slides.text: Your money has a carbon footprint. It's time to talk to your bank
When we talk about climate, we talk about technology, policy, and behaviour. But there is another dimension far less discussed:
We need both public and private money to finance the climate transition. No government can do it alone.
bullets: It's estimated $9.2 trillion are needed every year until 2050 to reach net zero (McKinsey)
But every $1 invested in climate resilience can return up to $4 in benefits (World Bank)
slides.footer: So why are some banks still financing the wrong projects?

slides.text: Your money matters. Your bank does not just hold your money. It uses it. Every euro you deposit is lent out, many times over. A significant share goes to oil, gas, and deforestation.
slides.footer: Up to 30% of lending in some banks. You don't see it. You don't sign off on it. But it happens every day.

slides.caption: €1,000 held in a carbon-intensive bank generates the same yearly emissions as a return flight from New York to Seattle. For most people, banking choices produce more indirect emissions than their flights.
slides.bold: flight from New York to Seattle

slides.caption: All put together, $3.8 trillion were provided to fossil fuel companies by the 60 largest banks since the Paris Agreement in 2015.
slides.note: While 29 of the 30 largest financiers had publicly committed to net zero.

slides.title: It's time to check what kind of bank you give your money to.
slides.badLabel: Those still funding the climate crisis
bad: Net zero pledges not matched by action
slides.goodLabel: Or those aligned with the transition
good: No financing to fossil fuel expansion

slides.caption: By switching to a climate-responsible bank, you could reduce the climate impact of your personal banking by 76%. One decision. No cost. No change to your daily life.
slides.note: Bigger impact than years of diet changes.

slides.text: The system is still funding the wrong things. You can choose which part of it you feed. Check your bank at bank.green or BankTrack — switch once and benefit for years.
